analogy.p: Imagine pushing the north poles of two strong magnets towards each other. They resist more and more as they get closer, so a gentle push just makes them bounce apart. If you throw them at each other really hard, they might get close enough to touch and snap together with a click. In fusion, positive nuclei repel like those magnets, so they must be thrown at each other at huge speed, which means very high temperature, and when they get close enough the strong nuclear force snaps them together and releases energy. The analogy breaks down because magnets just stick together and release only a little noise, whereas fusing nuclei form a new element and convert some mass into energy.

bullets: Know the definition: **nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus**.
Know that in fusion **some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation** (the exact mark-scheme wording).
Know that fusion happens naturally in **stars**, where hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium.
Know that fusion needs **very high temperature and pressure** to overcome the **electrostatic repulsion** between nuclei.
Be able to **compare fission and fusion**: size of nuclei, what happens, conditions needed and products.
Be able to **balance simple nuclear equations** for fusion using mass number and atomic number.
Be able to **evaluate** the use of fusion as a source of energy on Earth.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: This point is in the **Physics only (triple science)** content of AQA 4.4 Atomic structure, alongside fission. You must know that **nuclear fusion is the joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus**, and that in this process **some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation**. It matters because fusion powers the Sun and all stars and is the great hope for future clean energy, so it comes up in explain, compare and evaluate questions.

bullets: **Definition:** the **joining of two light nuclei** to form a **heavier nucleus**.
Typical examples use the hydrogen isotopes **deuterium (hydrogen-2)** and **tritium (hydrogen-3)**, which fuse to form **helium**.
Because the product is a different element, fusion is a **nuclear** change, not a chemical one.
In the process **some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation**: the products have slightly **less mass** than the starting nuclei.
Energy is released as **kinetic energy of the products** and as **gamma radiation**, which becomes thermal energy.
Fusion is the process that **powers the Sun and other stars**.
core.p: Fusion means joining. In **nuclear fusion**, two **light nuclei** (such as isotopes of hydrogen) come together to form **one heavier nucleus**. The new nucleus is a different element, and the reaction releases a very large amount of energy. It is the opposite of fission, which splits a large nucleus.

bullets: Nuclei are **positive**, so there is a **repulsive electrostatic force** between them.
The nuclei must be **close enough** for the **strong nuclear force** to pull them together. This force acts only over very short distances.
**High temperature** means the nuclei have **very high kinetic energy**, so they move fast enough to overcome the repulsion.
**High pressure** forces the nuclei **very close together** so fusion collisions are frequent.

**Temperature in the core of the Sun** is around 15 million degrees Celsius; fusion reactors on Earth need temperatures of the order of **100 million degrees Celsius** because the pressure is much lower than in a star.
At these temperatures the atoms are stripped of electrons and the material is a **plasma** (a gas of charged particles).
**Exam link:** 'Explain why fusion is hard to achieve' = high temperature needed to overcome electrostatic repulsion between positive nuclei.
core.h: Why fusion needs very high temperature and pressure
core.p: All nuclei are **positively charged**, so two nuclei **repel each other** with an **electrostatic force** that grows stronger as they get closer. To fuse, the nuclei must get so close that the **strong nuclear force** (a short-range attraction) takes over. That only happens if they collide at extremely high speed, which means an extremely high temperature. A high pressure squeezes the nuclei close together, so collisions happen often enough.

bullets: In the **core of a star**, hydrogen nuclei (protons) fuse in several steps to form **helium nuclei**, releasing energy.
**Gravity** provides the **high pressure and temperature** needed. No external heating is required.
The Sun is stable because **inward gravity is balanced by outward radiation and gas pressure**.
When hydrogen in the core runs low, heavier nuclei can fuse in larger stars, forming **heavier elements**.
**Fusion processes in stars produce all of the naturally occurring elements.** These may be spread through the Universe by the **explosion of a massive star (a supernova)**.
This links to the **life cycle of a star** in the Space physics topic.
core.p: Stars such as the Sun are huge balls of mostly hydrogen. The enormous **gravitational pull** squeezes the core to very high **pressure and temperature**, so hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium. The energy released heats the star and escapes as light and other radiation. A star stays stable because the outward pressure from the fusion energy balances the inward gravity.

bullets: **Equation (plain text):** H(2,1) + H(3,1) -> He(4,2) + n(1,0) + energy.
**Mass numbers:** left 2 + 3 = 5; right 4 + 1 = 5. They match.
**Atomic numbers:** left 1 + 1 = 2; right 2 + 0 = 2. They match.
**Deuterium** has 1 proton and 1 neutron; **tritium** has 1 proton and 2 neutrons; **helium-4** has 2 protons and 2 neutrons.
The **free neutron** carries away much of the energy; this is useful for heat but can make the reactor walls radioactive.
If a number is missing, **subtract**: unknown = total on one side - known values on the other.
The products here are **helium and a neutron**; helium itself is **stable, not radioactive**.
core.h: Fusion equations: balancing mass and atomic numbers
core.p: A standard example is the fusion of deuterium and tritium: H-2 + H-3 gives He-4 + a neutron + energy. As with fission, **total mass number** and **total atomic number** must be the same on both sides. Always check by adding the top numbers and the bottom numbers separately.

bullets: **Mark-scheme wording:** 'some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation'.
One D-T fusion releases about **17.6 MeV** of energy (a MeV is a million electronvolts).
For the same **mass of fuel**, fusion releases **roughly four times** more energy than fission (about 3.5 MeV per nucleon against about 0.85 MeV per nucleon for uranium-235).
**Higher-tier extension (beyond the spec wording):** the mass change is related to the energy released by E = mc^2, where c is the speed of light, so a very small mass gives a very large energy.
The energy is carried mostly as **kinetic energy** of the helium nucleus and neutron, which is then transferred as **thermal energy**.
This is the energy source that has kept the **Sun shining for billions of years**.
core.h: Where does the energy come from?
core.p: When the new nucleus forms, the total **mass** of the products is **slightly less** than the total mass of the original nuclei. The **missing mass is converted into energy** (the AQA phrase is that some of the mass may be converted into the energy of radiation). Because energy is released, the product nucleus is more stable than the starting nuclei. A tiny mass change gives a huge amount of energy.

bullets: **Nuclei used:** fission uses **large** nuclei (uranium-235, plutonium-239); fusion uses **small** nuclei (hydrogen isotopes).
**What happens:** fission **splits** one nucleus into **two smaller nuclei**; fusion **joins two nuclei into one heavier nucleus**.
**Conditions:** fission needs a **neutron** to be absorbed at normal temperature; fusion needs **extremely high temperature and pressure**.
**Neutrons:** fission releases **two or three neutrons** that can cause a **chain reaction**; fusion does **not** rely on a chain reaction.
**Waste:** fission products are **radioactive** with long half-lives; the main product of fusion (helium) is **not radioactive**.
**Fuel:** fission needs **mined uranium**; fusion fuel (deuterium) can be taken from **seawater**.
**Status:** fission is used widely **now**; fusion for electricity is still **experimental**.
core.p: Fission and fusion both release energy from the nucleus, but they work in opposite ways. Fission **splits a large unstable nucleus**; fusion **joins two light nuclei**. Fission starts by absorbing a neutron at ordinary temperatures; fusion needs enormous temperature and pressure. Examiners often ask you to compare them, so learn the differences as pairs.

bullets: **Main challenge:** reaching and **maintaining extremely high temperature and pressure** for long enough.
**Magnetic confinement:** the plasma is made of charged particles, so **magnetic fields** hold it in place away from the walls.
**Energy balance:** a power plant must produce **more energy out than is put in** to heat and contain the plasma, which has been very hard to achieve and keep up.
**Cost:** experimental reactors are **extremely expensive** to build and run.
If the conditions are lost the plasma **cools and fusion stops immediately**, so there is **no runaway chain reaction**.
Experimental devices include the **JET** and **ITER** tokamaks (named for context; you do not need to learn details).
core.h: Fusion as a source of energy on Earth
core.p: Scientists are trying to build **fusion reactors** to produce electricity, but it is very difficult. The fuel must be heated to over 100 million degrees Celsius and held in place long enough for fusion to occur. No material can touch something that hot, so the hot plasma is held away from the walls by **powerful magnetic fields** in doughnut-shaped devices such as **tokamaks**. Experimental reactors exist, but fusion is **not yet a commercial source of energy**.

bullets: **Advantages:** very **high energy output per kilogram of fuel**; fuel (hydrogen isotopes) is **plentiful**; **no carbon dioxide** released by the reaction.
**Advantages:** the main product, **helium**, is **not radioactive**, so **little long-lived radioactive waste** compared with fission.
**Advantages:** **safer in principle**: it cannot run out of control, because fusion stops if the conditions fail.
**Disadvantages:** **not yet a reliable source of electricity**; needs **extremely high temperature and pressure**.
**Disadvantages:** **very expensive** to research and build; the neutrons can make reactor parts **radioactive**.
For '**evaluate**' always give a **judgement**: for example 'fusion is promising but, until the technology works, fission and renewables must be used'.
core.p: A good evaluation sets out benefits and drawbacks and finishes with a judgement. Fusion would give huge amounts of energy from abundant fuel with little long-lived waste and no carbon dioxide, but the technology is not yet working at commercial scale, and the cost is very high.

bullets: This curve is **beyond the AQA GCSE specification**, but it explains the whole topic and helps with explain questions.
**Light nuclei** (hydrogen, helium) have **low binding energy per nucleon**, so fusing them moves **up** the curve and releases energy.
**Iron-56** is near the **peak**: it is among the **most stable nuclei**, so neither fusion nor fission of it releases energy.
**Heavy nuclei** (uranium) are on the **right-hand side**; splitting them gives nuclei **higher up** the curve, so fission releases energy.
This is why **stars cannot get energy by fusion beyond iron** and why the heavy elements need more than ordinary fusion to form.
**Rule of thumb:** energy is released when the products are **more stable** (higher binding energy per nucleon) than the starting nuclei.
core.p: Why does fusion release energy for light nuclei but fission for heavy ones? The answer is on the **binding energy per nucleon curve**. Binding energy is the energy needed to pull a nucleus apart; a higher value per nucleon means a **more stable** nucleus. The curve rises steeply for light nuclei, peaks around **iron-56**, and falls slowly for heavy nuclei. Moving **up the curve** towards iron releases energy, so **fusion of light nuclei** and **fission of heavy nuclei** both release energy.

bullets: **Space physics (4.8):** the Sun and stars form from clouds of dust and gas; **gravity** raises temperature and pressure until **fusion** begins and the star enters its **main sequence** stable period.
**Isotopes:** deuterium and tritium are **isotopes of hydrogen**: same number of protons (1), different numbers of neutrons (1 and 2).
**Energy resources:** a future fusion plant would be **low carbon** and produce very large amounts of energy from small amounts of fuel.
**Electrostatics link:** like charges **repel**, which is why nuclei need such high kinetic energy to get close.
**Particle model link:** higher temperature means higher average **kinetic energy** of particles, so more collisions happen with enough energy to fuse.
**Radiation link:** gamma radiation is emitted, which is an **electromagnetic wave**.
core.p: Fusion connects physics topics. It explains how the Sun produces its energy, connects to **isotopes** and **nuclear equations**, and is linked to **energy resources** because it could be a future low-carbon source.

bullets: **Fusion = join** two light nuclei into a heavier nucleus.
**Needs** very high temperature and pressure to overcome **electrostatic repulsion**.
**Energy released** because some mass is converted to energy of radiation.
**Happens in stars**: hydrogen to helium in the core.
**On Earth** fusion is still **experimental**: hard to heat and contain plasma.
**Compared with fission:** fusion is **cleaner** and uses plentiful fuel but is **not yet practical**.
core.p: If you remember one thing: **fusion joins light nuclei** into a heavier one, needs **very high temperature and pressure**, releases energy because **some mass is converted to energy of radiation**, and powers **stars**. Fission is the reverse: **splits large nuclei**. Use this short summary to check you can state each fact.

exam: **Define it (1 mark):** 'The joining of two light nuclei to form a heavier nucleus.' Say light and heavier.
**Where does the energy come from (1 to 2 marks):** 'some of the mass is converted into energy (of radiation)'. Use this exact idea.
**Why high temperature (2 to 3 marks):** nuclei are positive and repel; high temperature gives high kinetic energy so they can get close enough to fuse.
**Why high pressure (1 mark):** to force the nuclei very close together so collisions are frequent.

**Compare fission and fusion (3 to 4 marks):** fission splits a large nucleus, fusion joins two small nuclei; fission needs a neutron, fusion needs very high temperature; fission waste is radioactive, fusion product is helium.
**Nuclear equations (2 marks):** add top numbers and bottom numbers on both sides and show the totals match.
**Stars (2 to 3 marks):** gravity compresses the core, giving high temperature and pressure, so hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium and release energy.

**Evaluate fusion reactors (6 marks):** give advantages (plentiful fuel, no carbon dioxide, little long-lived waste) and disadvantages (not yet practical, very high temperature, very expensive) plus a judgement.
**Command words:** 'state' = a fact; 'describe' = what happens; 'explain' = what happens and why; 'compare' = similarities and differences using linking words such as 'whereas'.
**Keywords to include:** light nuclei, heavier nucleus, high temperature, high pressure, electrostatic repulsion, mass converted into energy.

worked.ans: Model answer: Nuclei are positive and repel each other. For fusion they must get close enough for the strong nuclear force to act, so they need very high kinetic energy, which means a very high temperature. On Earth it is hard to reach and maintain temperatures of over 100 million degrees Celsius and to contain the plasma, because no material can touch it, so magnetic fields are needed. This makes fusion reactors very difficult and expensive.
worked.q: Explain why nuclear fusion requires a very high temperature, and why it is difficult to achieve in a power station on Earth. (4 marks)
steps: Nuclei are positively charged so they repel each other (electrostatic repulsion).
They must get very close for the strong nuclear force to join them.
High temperature gives the nuclei high kinetic energy to overcome the repulsion.
On Earth the temperature (over 100 million degrees Celsius) and pressure must be maintained, and the hot plasma must be held away from walls using magnetic fields.
